units.text: Moral agent. A being to whom we can address reasons and to whom we can attribute actions in a sense relevant to moral evaluation. The exact conditions of this status are disputed; merely producing an effect is not enough.
Morally considerable person or being. Someone whose interests matter in justifying our conduct. Having this status does not necessarily entail the capacity to answer morally for one's own acts.
Causal responsibility. Contribution to bringing about an outcome. It does not automatically entail intention, sufficient control, blame, or an obligation to punish.
Retrospective responsibility. Assessment of what an agent did or omitted to do, and of the grounds for praise, criticism, or blame.
Prospective responsibility. The obligation to act in the future: prevention, protection, verification, or coordination. It can exist without blame for the origin of the problem.
Role responsibility. Obligations attached to a position or relationship. The role must itself be justified and does not automatically override other moral demands.
Reparative responsibility. The obligation to redress, compensate for, or acknowledge harm. Reparation does not mean that every loss can be undone.
Legal liability. An obligation or consequence established within a framework of law and procedures. It is not synonymous with the general moral assessment of a person.

Being accountable. Being open to questions about a decision and required to provide explanations, information, and, where appropriate, corrections. A simple declaration of accepting responsibility does not exhaust this relationship.
Excuse and justification. An excuse may reduce the agent's blame without making the action good. A justification maintains that the action was permitted or required in the circumstances.
Moral luck. The influence of unchosen factors on the situations, consequences, or characteristics for which people are morally evaluated.
Compatibilism. The family of positions according to which a relevant form of freedom and responsibility can be compatible with determinism. It does not assume that every constraint is unimportant.
Culpable ignorance. Ignorance for which there are grounds for reproach, because the agent had the relevant opportunity and obligation to become informed. Not all ignorance falls into this category.
Special obligation. A requirement connected to specific promises, roles, or relationships, distinct from what we would owe any person. The limits of legitimate partiality remain disputed.
Supererogation. A morally good action that exceeds what is obligatory. Where this boundary lies, especially in helping those in need, is one of the book's central disputes.
Problem of evil. The family of arguments examining the relationship between the existence and nature of suffering and certain conceptions of divine power, knowledge, and goodness.
